Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Wildlife Management Unit 116 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Alberta Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 116 (Seven Persons 
WMU) is located generally southwest of Medicine Hat, and 
covers an area of approximately 2,096 km2. The majority of the 
unit is within Alberta’s dry mixed-grass natural subregion, with 
the southeast portion near the Cypress Hills extending in to the 
mixed-grass natural subregion. The WMU includes the area 
commencing at the junction of highways 1 and 3 at Medicine 
Hat; thence southwesterly and westerly along highway 3 to 
secondary road 885; thence southerly along highway 885 to 
highway 61; thence southerly and easterly along highway 61 to 
secondary road 889; thence northerly along secondary road 889 
(locally known as the Black and White Trail) for approximately 
20 km to the road locally known as the Ranchville Road, thence 
easterly and northeasterly along the Ranchville Road to Eagle 
Butte Road at the southeast corner of township 8, range 4, west 
of the fourth meridian; thence northwesterly and northerly along 
this road to highway 1; thence northwesterly along highway 1 
to the point of commencement. Several drainages containing 
large coulee systems originate in the Cypress Hills and extend 
westward and northward through the WMU, including Peigan 
Creek, Bullshead Creek, and Seven Persons Creek. Land is 
primarily deeded, and general habitat and land use consists of 
cultivated cropland for the purpose of annual crop production, 
and tame and native grassland used for cattle grazing. Some 
parcels of crown owned native grassland under grazing lease 
are also present. Oil and gas development is established 
throughout the WMU, and in recent years, renewable energy 
development has also increased. Chronic Wasting disease is 
well established within the WMU, with an overall prevalence 
of 20.69 per cent in 2022. Furthermore, submitted samples 
showed prevalence rates of 34.62 per cent in mule deer bucks 
and 9.38 per cent in mule deer does in 2022.
The established pre-hunting season population goal for WMU 
116 is 2145 mule deer and 1080 white-tailed deer. Ungulate 
harvest in WMU 116 is currently managed using a special 
license draw for antlered and antlerless mule deer, antlerless 
white-tailed deer, elk, and moose. During the archery 
only season, antlered white-tailed deer and mule deer are 
hunted with general licenses, which are available without the 
requirement of a Special License obtained through the draw 
process. Landowner licenses for mule deer and antlerless elk 
are also available to eligible residents.
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and 
moose) was last conducted for WMU 116 in 2003 using the 
modified Gassaway/random stratified block methodology 
(Random Block) (Table 1). With over 20 years since the last 
survey, an updated population estimate is needed to ensure 
management goals are based on more relevant data. It 
is important to consider the difference in methods when 
comparing results between the surveys.
The objective of the February 2024 survey was to assess the 
status of the ungulate population in WMU 116 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. 
We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including elk, pronghorn, 
carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at-risk species.
Survey Method
A rotary wing transect survey was conducted February 9–11, 
2024 flying 37 east-west lines at 1.85 km intervals, with  
48 per cent coverage (800 m wide survey strip, area surveyed 
1003 km2) for a total linear survey effort of 1254 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by species, and 
when possible, sex and age were recorded. Antler size for 
deer was classified as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or 
both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers 
inside ears), or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of 
ears).
Because transects varied in length, the average density 
(R; #/km2) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose was 
calculated by multiplying the number of animals per transect 
(∑x) by total area searched (total survey strip area [∑z]) (Jolly 
1969, as described in Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was 
multiplied by the WMU (Z) area to determine population 
estimates with a 90 per cent confidence intervals. Confidence 
interval width was calculated by multiplying the t statistic for 
the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t 0.05,df=n-1) 
by standard error (SE; without replacement) of the abundance 
estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/
(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of 
possible transects given 100 per cent coverage, and n as the 
number of transects sampled.
Moose and Elk observations made during the survey were 
also recorded. Elk population estimates were part of a 
concurrent minimum total count (MTC) survey of the Cypress 
Hills elk herd (WMU 624 and surrounding area) and are 
presented in another report. Moose observations were used 
to calculate an estimate for the small but well-established 
moose population found in the WMU.

Results
A total of 782 mule deer were observed with an average 
groups size of 5 (range 1-23). The estimated density was 
0.78 mule deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 1,634 
individuals (90 per cent CI 1,263 – 2,005). A total of 630 mule 
deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio 
was estimated to be 49:100:78. That results in an estimated 
2024 winter mule deer population of 352 bucks, 718 does, 
and 564 fawns. Of the 131 mule deer bucks classified, 46 (34 
per cent) were classified ‘small’, 45 (33 per cent) ‘medium’, 
and 45 (33 per cent) ‘large’. The 2024 population estimate 
represents a 9 per cent decrease from the last aerial ungulate 
survey population estimate for mule deer within WMU 116 
(conducted in 2003). However, the survey in 2024 showed 
increases in both buck to doe and fawn to do ratios (Table 1). 
When comparing survey results, it is important to note that 
the last survey used a different survey methodology (modified 
Gassaway/random block).
A total of 289 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 6 (range 1-34). The estimated density 
was 0.29 deer/km2 and the estimated abundance was 
604 individuals (90 per cent CI 198 – 1,010). A total of 113 
white-tailed deer were successfully classified and the bucks: -
does:fawns ratio was estimated to be 24:100:106. That results 
in an estimated 2023 early winter white-tailed deer population 
of 64 bucks, 262 does, and 278 fawns. Of the 12 white-tailed 
deer bucks classified, 5 (42 per cent) were classified ‘small’, 
6 (50 per cent) ‘medium’, and 1 (8 per cent) ‘large’. The 
2024 population estimate represents a 36 per cent increase 
when compared to 2003 data, however once again different 
methodologies were used between surveys, so results are not 
directly comparable. Furthermore, it is likely some antler shed 
had occurred in white-tailed deer, so sex rations should be 
interpreted with caution. Age/sex data was not available for 
comparison for white-tailed deer from the 2003 survey.
A total of 14 moose were observed with and average group 
size of 1 (range 1-2). The estimated density was 0.014 moose/
km2 and the estimated abundance was 29 individuals (90 per 
cent CI 14 – 44). Moose were generally confined to brushy 
creek valleys and associated coulees as suitable moose 
habitat is generally limited in prairie WMUs.
A total of 606 pronghorn were observed during the survey. 
Other species observed included elk, sharp-tailed grouse, 
gray partridge, ring-necked pheasant, bald eagle, and coyote.
